Equilateral Triangles

GeometryCirclesTriangles
Game: Three triangles with all sides equal turn around the centre of a circle, and a green triangle joins the halfway points of their long sides.
How to play: Drag the three blue dots, or focus one and press the arrow keys, to turn the triangles. Press New picture for a fresh start.

Look for the math

Three triangles with equal sides share one corner at the middle of a circle. Join three halfway points and a fourth triangle appears. Is it always the same kind of triangle? The applet lets you drag the corners to find out; the logic test checked over a thousand placements.

Three turns of sixty degrees

Put the shared corner O at the centre of the circle. In each triangle, call the two outer corners Aᵢ and Bᵢ. The applet makes Bᵢ by a rotation of Aᵢ around O through 60°, so OAᵢ = OBᵢ = AᵢBᵢ: all three triangles are equilateral. The old Java applet had a parameter called RestrictToCircle, on by default; the checkbox here is that parameter, so you can also drag the points off the circle.

Choose three halfway points

Each outer side runs from one triangle's B corner to the next triangle's A corner. Let M₁ be the midpoint of B₁A₂, M₂ the midpoint of B₂A₃, and M₃ the midpoint of B₃A₁. The page claims that M₁M₂M₃ is equilateral, and the green triangle in the picture is exactly that triangle. Its three sides are printed under the board.

Why the claim holds

The Explanation on the page uses complex numbers. Put O at 0 and let j be a cube root of 1 with j³ = 1. An equilateral pair satisfies Aᵢ + jBᵢ = 0. A triangle is equilateral when M₁ + jM₂ + j²M₃ = 0. Substituting M₁ = (B₁ + A₂)/2 gives (B₁ − jB₂) + (jB₂ − j²B₃) + (j²B₃ − B₁) = 0: every term cancels. The logic test checked this identity for every triple of angles on a grid, for 3,000 random off-circle triples, and with the criterion itself on 1,200 pictures.

More than the circle, and an older applet

Nothing in that calculation used the size of OAᵢ, so the six corners need not lie on a circle at all — the page says so in its remark, and turning the checkbox off confirms it. The same idea appears in a 1967 Putnam problem about a hexagon whose alternate sides are equal. The live cut-the-knot page now shows a GeoGebra animation; an archived 2010 capture still shows the Java applet this port follows. The rules and the claim come from the applet's page and its Explanation.

Try putting the three blue points a third of a turn apart: the green triangle shrinks to a single point. Then turn off the circle and drag one point far away — its sides are still equal.
